title: Friendship with Jesus (II.8)
hook: without a friend you can't live well; let Jesus be your friend
tomorrow: who's still there when the party's over?

segments.voice: Yesterday: love all for Jesus, and Jesus for himself, so nobody gets demoted, and love doesn't fall when things fall. The line was above all.

A voice note from a friend far away. Before the name even loads, the voice is already home: the laugh at the start, the way it says hey. A person can be close to someone they can't see. The ear knows first. John's Gospel has a moment built on that. A house in Bethany, full of mourners. A woman sits grieving her brother. Her sister Martha leans close and says quietly that the master is here, and is calling for her. She gets up at once. She doesn't wait.
screen: `A VOICE NOTE FROM FAR AWAY.` → `THE EAR KNOWS FIRST.` → `THE MASTER IS CALLING FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: The Imitation stops right on that moment, in chapter eight of book two. When Jesus is near, it says, all is well and nothing seems hard. When he seems far, everything is hard. If he speaks just one word, the comfort is great. John calls the woman Mary, Martha's sister; the Imitation, following an older way of reading, calls her Mary Magdalene. Either way, the point is the rising: one familiar voice, and she's on her feet. Her grief doesn't vanish; she still weeps when she reaches him. But she moves toward the voice. Then the chapter calls it an art. It's a great art, it says, to know how to talk with Jesus, and great wisdom to keep him close. Be humble and peaceable, and he'll be with you; be devout and quiet, and he'll stay. Then the line at the chapter's heart: without a friend, the book says, you can't live well. It doesn't call loneliness a virtue. It says if Jesus isn't your friend above all, you'll be very sad and desolate. And its title uses an old word, familiar, in an older sense: close, at home with you, of the household. Not a distant master you book an appointment with. A friend whose voice you know before the name loads.
screen: `NEAR, ALL IS WELL.` · `ONE WORD, AND SHE RISES.` · `A GREAT ART: TALKING WITH JESUS.` · `A FRIEND OF THE HOUSE.` · then, large: `WITHOUT A FRIEND YOU CAN'T LIVE WELL.`

segments.voice: Say a few words out loud, quietly, the way you'd talk to a close friend at the end of a day: one thing that happened, one thing that was hard. If you pray, say them to Jesus; if you don't, say them to the room and notice how a spoken thought sounds different. Plain words are enough. Then let the quiet answer.
Friendship with Jesus. The Imitation's familiar friend: close enough to talk with plainly, and kept near by being humble, peaceable and quiet.
The line to keep: a familiar friend, close enough that you never have to knock. See you soon.

howItsDone: Many Catholics practice mental prayer, speaking to Christ in their own words as to a friend, and some make a short visit to a church to sit quietly before the tabernacle.

notes: Imitation II.8 paraphrased: when Jesus is present all is good and nothing seems hard, when absent all is hard; one word from him brings great consolation; Mary Magdalene rose at once when Martha said 'The master is here and calls you'; it is a great art to know how to converse with Jesus and great wisdom to keep him; be humble and peaceable, devout and quiet, and he will stay; without a friend you cannot live well, and if Jesus is not your friend above all you will be very sad and desolate. Confirm each against the Latin.

The Imitation names the woman Mary Magdalene; John 11 calls her Mary, Martha's sister. The lesson says so plainly and calls the identification 'an older way of reading'. Confirm the wording is fair. 'Familiar' in its older sense (of the household) is stated as meaning, not etymology.
Latin 'familiaris amicitia' is offered as the nominative form of the chapter title 'De familiari amicitia Iesu'. Confirm.
